title: TA9-14690
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXX XXXX XXXX XXXX ("principal claimant"), and her minor daughter, XXXXXX XXXXX XXXXX ("minor claimant"), citizens of Mexico, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act.1 The claimants' identities have been established through identity documents filed in evidence.2

The minor claimant bases her claim on the claim of the principal claimant's (file number TA9-14690) Personal Information Form (PIF) narrative.3 The principal claimant was appointed the Designated Representative of the minor claimant.

In making the assessment in this case, I considered the Chairperson's Gender Guidelines4 to ensure that warranted accommodations were made in terms of questioning the principal claimant and the overall hearing process.
The following is a summary of the principal claimant's allegations:

The principal claimant was sexually abused by her father from the age of four to ten years old. The principal claimant was married to XXXX in 1980, when she was 24-years-old. During the course of their marriage, XXXX physically and sexually assaulted the principal claimant. XXXX was an alcoholic and drug user and threatened to kill the claimant on a number of occasions. The couple divorced on XXXX, 2006, but XXXX continued to threaten the principal claimant after they were divorced. The principal claimant called the police on XXXX approximately 50 times during their relationship. The police would remove XXXX from the home and would sometimes detain him. When XXXX was jailed, his family members would coerce the principal claimant to withdraw her complaint against him. The claimants fled Mexico on XXXX, 2009 and filed claims for refugee protection on June 15, 2009.

I find that the claimants have not satisfied the burden of establishing a serious possibility of persecution on a Convention ground, or that they would personally be subjected, on a balance of probabilities, to a danger of torture, or a risk to life or a risk of cruel and unusual treatment or punishment upon return to their country. Therefore, I find that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the IRPA.

In arriving at my decision, I considered the issue of whether the claimants' fear is objectively reasonable. In this regard, I considered whether or not there is adequate state protection in Mexico, whether the claimants took all reasonable steps to avail themselves of that protection, and whether they have provided clear and convincing evidence of the state's inability to protect. ANALYSIS Procedural Issue - Reasonable Apprehension of Bias

Following the hearing, counsel submitted a motion for the member to recuse himself due to a reasonable apprehension of bias. Counsel argues that XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX .
I have carefully considered counsel's motion regarding this matter. In addition I have also considered the relevant jurisprudence.
For the following reasons, the Application for Recusal is denied.

Prior to the hearing, counsel requested that the hearing be postponed because she had only recently been retained by the claimants and required additional time to prepare. The Board denied counsel's written request for a postponement prior to the hearing indicating that the claimant has been in Canada for over one year and has had ample time to retain and instruct counsel. Considering that counsel was informed that her postponement request had been denied, prior to the hearing, she should have been prepared to proceed with the hearing on the date scheduled.

Counsel submitted an extensive disclosure package two days prior to the hearing containing: * over 100 pages of country condition documents * a Mexican police report * a new eight page narrative for the principal claimant * amendments to the principal claimant's Personal Information Form
Since a portion of the disclosure was claim specific and probative and in fairness to the claimants, the member waived the 20-day rule and allowed the documents into evidence.

At the hearing, which commenced at 1:00 p.m., counsel requested that the hearing be postponed due to her being retained just two weeks prior. Counsel was asked if there were any other reasons for her request for a postponement, other than the ones given in writing, that the Board had already ruled on. Counsel indicated that her client had not received the Board's disclosure package and that she confirmed with the Case Management Officer's supervisor, one day prior to the hearing, that her client was not sent the disclosure package. The member reviewed the file and indicated to counsel that the disclosure package was sent to the claimant and her previous counsel of record on August 13, 2009. Even though the member confirmed that disclosure was made to the claimant and previous counsel, a copy of the disclosure package was made for counsel at the time of the hearing. The member denied counsel's request for a postponement and proceeded with the hearing. Throughout the hearing, counsel reiterated her request for a postponement indicating that she had not had ample time to review the disclosure material. The member kept reminding counsel with a measured tone that the issue had been dealt with and instructed her to proceed with the hearing.

Counsel advised the member during the hearing that she could stay no later than 4:00 p.m. The member was prepared to stay as long as required to complete the hearing. The principal claimant was questioned by the member from 1:50 p.m. to 2:30 p.m. The member called a break at 2:30 p.m. and asked that all parties reconvene at 2:45 p.m. Upon the resumption of the hearing, the member advised counsel that she could question the claimants until 3:30 p.m. at which time she would provide her submissions orally. The member gave counsel the option of questioning until 4:00 p.m., and providing the member with written submissions within two weeks of the hearing. There was also the option to continue the hearing beyond 4:00 p.m., until it was concluded.

Counsel questioned the principal claimant from 2:45 p.m. until 3:30 p.m. At 3:30, the member reminded counsel that she had one half hour left for questions or submissions. Counsel advised the member that she may not be able to conclude her questions by 4:00 p.m. Counsel was reminded that she was expected to conclude the hearing that day and was offered a five-minute recess to formulate her questions for the remaining time. As the member was about to leave the hearing room for the recess, counsel XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX XXXXXXX. Counsel did not return for the conclusion of the hearing. The member informed the claimants that he would write to counsel and instruct her to provide written submissions within two weeks and would also consider counsel's submissions on why she believes that there are other areas of questioning that still need to be done.

The member took the necessary measures to conduct the hearing in an efficient and fair manner. Counsel made many attempts during the hearing to have the proceeding postponed or adjourned. Counsel continued to repeat the same motions and objections even after they were dealt with and decided upon by the member. Counsel would not accept the rulings. The member XXXX XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

Counsel submits that the occurrences that took place at the hearing give rise, individually and collectively, to a reasonable apprehension of bias. She also indicates that much questioning of the claimants remains.

The Federal Court of Appeal stated the following in XXXX:5 XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX has been accepted in this country as expressing the modern test for determining the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias. Adopting the formulation proposed by this Court, he said (at pages XXX-XXX): The proper test to be applied in a matter of this type was correctly expressed by the Court of Appeal. As already seen by the quotation above, the apprehension of bias must be a reasonable one, held by reasonable and right minded persons, applying themselves to the question and obtaining thereon the required information. In the words of the Court of Appeal, that test is "what would an informed person, viewing the matter realistically and practically - and having thought the matter through - conclude. Would he think that it is more likely than not that [the decision-maker], whether consciously or unconsciously, would not decide fairly." I can see no real difference between the expressions found in the decided cases, be they 'reasonable apprehension of bias', 'reasonable suspicion of bias', or 'real likelihood of bias'. The grounds for this apprehension must, however, be substantial and I entirely agree with the Federal Court of Appeal which refused to accept the suggestion that the test be related to the "very sensitive or scrupulous conscience".

Thus, the impartiality of decision-makers is not judged from the decision-maker's perspective, but from that of a reasonable bystander, fully informed of all relevant facts. As stated by the Supreme Court of Canada,6 "The test for apprehension of bias takes into account the presumption of impartiality. A real likelihood of bias must be demonstrated."

The test for a perceived apprehension of biased is a high one because there is a presumption that those who are appointed to judicial or quasi-judicial office are able to put behind them any affiliations or prejudices they may have held at that time. The Federal Court held that: The basic premise on which the credibility of this system are maintained is that all Canadian citizens who hold judicial or quasi-judicial office leave behind them whatever baggage of earlier affiliations or prejudices - tribal, religious, racial, cultural or otherwise - which they might have hitherto carried. ... It is an aberration to suggest that [the Member], who arrived in Canada in 1968 and became a Canadian citizen in 1976, cannot, by reason of ancestral warfare and conflict, carry out properly, objectively and judicially the duties and responsibilities which parliament has imposed upon him.7

Furthermore, the Court has also stated: Judges do not descend from heaven. They come from various fields of activities. Some of us are former academics, others were in the public service, others practiced law in small towns or large firms. And some of us were in politics. The variety of our individual careers is a rich source of knowledge and experience for the courts. Once we took our oath of office, we divorced ourselves from our past and dedicated ourselves to our new vocation. Our duty is to render justice without fear or favours.8

As in the case formerly cited, all members of the Refugee Protection Division of the Immigration and Refugee Board (IRB) have taken an oath of office prior to the commencement of their duties which, in part, affirms, "(a) I will, during the term of my appointment, and any re-appointments, faithfully, impartially and to the best of my knowledge and ability, properly carry out the duties of a full-time Member of the Immigration and Refugee Board of Canada; and (b) I will comply with the Code of Conduct for Members."9 The Code of Conduct for Members10 is based on the Board's dedication to the following values: honesty, good faith, fairness, accountability, dignity, respect, transparency, openness, discretion, cultural sensitivity and loyalty. These standards address Member's responsibilities to the tribunal itself, including colleagues and staff, to the parties who appear before them, and to the public (paragraphs 6 and 7). The Code also states: 28. Members shall make each decision on the merits of the case, based on thorough preparation, the assessment of the evidence properly before the Member and the application of the relevant law. The relevant law consists of the Act, the Canadian Charter of Rights and Freedoms, other relevant legislation, regulations, legal principles, including the principles of natural justice, and the relevant case law. ... 29. Members shall not be influenced by extraneous or improper considerations in their decision-making. Members shall make their decisions free from the improper influence of other persons, institutions, interest groups or the political process.

Therefore, the test for apprehension of bias takes into account the presumption of impartiality. A real likelihood of bias must be demonstrated.11 The Supreme Court reiterated this principle when it stated that the standard refers to an apprehension of bias that rests on serious grounds, in light of the strong presumption of judicial impartiality.12

In XXXX,13 the Minister brought an application for judicial review for a decision of an Immigration Appeals Division (IAD) Member on the grounds of apprehension of bias arising from the allegation that the Member XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX Minister's counsel at the IAD hearing regarding her inability to stay late to complete the hearing. The applicant put forth the following points of issue: Did the Member's conduct give rise to a reasonable apprehension of bias? Did the Member's conduct interfere with the Minister's ability to participate? Was there a breach in procedural fairness? In response, the Respondent (appellant before the IAD) argued that the Minister's XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.
XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX: .
In this case XX "XXXXXXX" XXXX XXXXXX the Member.

XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX: XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX. XXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXXX.

The Court supports a member's authority to be firm and measured with counsel with respect to the conduct of a hearing. Counsel's actions and provocations must be dealt with sternly when they are seen to be disruptive to the proceeding. Counsel's decision to walk out of the hearing prevented her from completing her questions to the claimants. It was not the member's decision to prevent counsel from presenting her case.

Counsel submits that she was unable to question the minor claimant and that these questions relate to the core issues of state protection and IFA. Notwithstanding the fact that the member directed counsel to conclude her questioning of the principal claimant and the minor claimant, however she saw fit, the minor claimant bases her claim on the claim of her mother, the principal claimant. The principal claimant was also appointed the Designated Representative of the minor claimant. The significant events of the claims directly involve the principal claimant and XXXX. The minor claimant's claim is inextricably tied to the principal claimant's claim. No persuasive evidence was presented to indicate that the minor claimant's testimony was critical in the determination of these claims. As such, I find that counsel's request to examine the minor claimant is unnecessary.

I have carefully considered all the relevant issues in this motion. I have directed my mind to the test for determining the existence of a reasonable apprehension of bias. Counsel has not demonstrated that the apprehension of bias is a reasonable one, held by reasonable and right minded persons, applying themselves to the question and obtaining thereon the required information. Furthermore, the claimant's apprehensions, arising out of these same factors, do not give rise to a breach of natural or fundamental justice. In light of the above noted reasons and the strong presumption of judicial impartiality, the motion for recusal is therefore denied. State Protection

The Board, in assessing the issue of state protection, is guided by a number of cases from the Supreme Court of Canada and the Federal Court. The courts have established a number of principles relating to state protection and I have applied those principles to the case at hand.

There is a presumption that, except in situations where the state is in complete breakdown, the state is capable of protecting its citizens. The presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens underscores the principle that international protection comes into play only when a refugee claimant has no other recourse available. Having canvassed the country conditions documents, I find that Mexico is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. The country has an estimated 2,600 police forces with approximately 400,000 officers operating at the municipal, state, and federal levels. During the year the government deployed approximately 50,000 military in 10 states to support, and in some municipalities to coordinate, the fight against the country's well-armed and well-funded organized criminal groups. The government continues its long-term effort to reform and improve the country's police organizations, with the goal of replacing the military in its domestic law enforcement function.14

To rebut the presumption of state protection, a claimant must provide "clear and convincing" evidence of the state's inability to protect its citizens.15 A claimant who alleges that state protection is inadequate must persuade the Board that the evidence establishes that the state protection is in fact, inadequate. The evidence that state protection is inadequate must not only be reliable and probative, it must also satisfy the Board, on a balance of probabilities, that state protection is inadequate.16 Where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authority in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact that the state's efforts are not always successful will not rebut the presumption of state protection.17 A claimant cannot rebut the presumption of state protection in a functioning democracy by asserting only a subjective reluctance to engage the state.18 Doubting the effectiveness of the protection offered by the state when one has not really tested it does not rebut the existence of a presumption of state protection.19

Refugee protection is meant to be a form of surrogate protection to be invoked only in those situations where the refugee claimant has unsuccessfully sought the protection of their home state. The onus is on the claimant to approach the state for protection in situations where state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.20 In the absence of a compelling explanation, a failure to pursue state protection opportunities within the home state will usually be fatal to a refugee claim, at least where the state is a functioning democracy with a willingness and the apparatus necessary to provide a measure of protection to its citizens.21

The claimant's burden of proof is directly proportional to the level of democracy in the state in question: the more democratic the state's institutions, the more the claimant must have done to exhaust all courses of action open to them.22 In a functioning democracy, a claimant will have a heavy burden when attempting to show that they should not have been required to exhaust all of the recourses available to them domestically before claiming refugee status.23 The documentary evidence24 before the Board indicates that Mexico is a democracy, and there are free and fair elections. There is a relatively independent and impartial judiciary. Therefore, in countries such as Mexico, the claimant must do more than merely show that he or she went to see Members of the police force and that those efforts were unsuccessful. A claimant must show that they have taken all reasonable steps in the circumstances to seek protection, taking into account the context of the country of origin, the steps taken and the claimant's interactions with the authorities.25 Local failures by authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of the state's inability or refusal to provide protection.26 No government is expected to guarantee perfect protection to all of its citizens at all times, and the fact that a state is not always successful in protecting its citizens, is not enough to justify a claim, especially where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and is making serious efforts to protect its citizens.27 Less than perfect protection is not a basis to determine that a state is either unwilling or unable to offer reasonable protection.28
In view of these principles, the principal claimant was questioned as to what efforts she made to seek state protection before fleeing Mexico.

The principal claimant testified that she called the police to take XXXX away on many occasions. When asked if the police responded every time she called them, the principal claimant indicated that the police would always show up, albeit late. When asked what the police would do when they responded to her calls, the principal claimant stated that she told the police to take XXXX away and the police would do so and tell her to go file a complaint. The principal claimant went on to say that she never filed a complaint against XXXX because she feared what he would do if she did. The principal claimant writes the following in her Personal Information Form narrative:29 I called the police on him about 50 times. They would take care of him by taking out (sic) of the house and sometimes they detained him. His mother would force me to go to jail and withdraw the complaint.

When asked about the complaint she filed against XXXX on XXXX, 2004, the principal claimant testified that XXXX was incarcerated and later released on XXXX pesos bail. When asked why she withdrew her complaint, the principal claimant indicated that XXXX and his family Members threatened her and XXXX brother offered her money to withdraw her complaint. When asked if she reported these threats and bribe to the police, the principal claimant stated that she did not; after she realized he was released on 2,000 pesos bail, she did not think she could do anything against XXXX relatives. When asked if she requested a restraining order against XXXX, the principal claimant stated that restraining orders do not exist in Mexico. When counsel asked the principal claimant about the first time she tried to get help, she testified that it was in 1984, four years after her marriage that she had the courage to call the police. When asked if the police came, the principal claimant indicated that the municipal police assigned to her neighbourhood arrived and she told them that her husband had beaten her up. XXXX had left the house when the claimant called the police. The principal claimant told the police not to leave and to patrol around the house. The police asked the principal claimant for XXXX physical description. The principal claimant went on to say that the police would do rounds and stop in front of the house. The police also gave her a telephone number to use in case of emergency. She testified that she did not use the telephone number as XXXX did not return that day but called two days later asking for forgiveness.

I find that the police responded to the principal claimant's calls for assistance each time she called them. The police told the principal claimant to file a report each time they responded. The principal claimant failed to file a report on all but one occasion because she feared what XXXX might do to her. I find that the reason the principal claimant failed to file complaints against XXXX is unreasonable. XXXX would have been incarcerated and prosecuted if the principal claimant filed any complaint against him. The one occasion the claimant filed a report against XXXX, he was incarcerated. XXXX was released on bail and he and his family members threatened and tried to bribe the principal claimant to withdraw her complaint. The principal claimant withdrew her complaint against XXXX because she was afraid that he would act on his threats to her. The principal claimant failed to advise the police about XXXX and his family's threats and attempted bribe after she filed the complaint.

I also find that the police provided the claimants with adequate protection. The police responded each time they were called, they removed the aggressor from the home, they instructed the victim to file a complaint and they arrested and charged the aggressor the one time the victim filed a complaint. A female police officer was assigned to take the principal claimant's report when she went to file the complaint. Police sent the principal claimant to their doctor to be examined. The principal claimant's decision to not report the threats and bribes after XXXX was arrested and her withdrawal of the complaint against him thwarted the attempts of the police to investigate, prosecute and convict XXXX. The principal claimant was responsible, in part, for not pursuing actions against XXXX. The principal claimant feared what XXXX and his family members might do to her if she reported them or did not withdraw her complaint against XXXX. I find that it was unreasonable for her not to report the further threats and bribes and to withdraw her complaint against XXXX because the police were taking the appropriate measures to protect the principal claimant and no persuasive evidence was presented to indicate that the police would not take further action if the threats and bribes were also reported to them.

Counsel submits that the principal claimant was afraid to file a formal police report because XXXX brother, XXXX XXXX, was a Federal Police officer and XXXX would find out that she filed a report. I find that XXXX XXXX role as a police officer had little effect on the principal claimant's ability to file a complaint. XXXX became aware of the principal claimant's call to the police each time they were called because the police removed him from the house after each reported incident and he was also jailed on occasion. XXXX also became aware of the principal claimant's complaint against him because the police apprehended him and advised him what he was being accused of. Furthermore, no persuasive evidence was presented to indicate that XXXX XXXX had any influence over the decisions of police. The attempt by XXXX family to bribe the principal claimant to withdraw her complaint demonstrates that XXXX XXXX did not have any influence over the police to investigate and prosecute XXXX.

I am not persuaded that the police would not act on the principal claimant's further allegations of XXXX and his family's threats and bribes since they had acted on all of her previous reports to them. I am also not persuaded that the police would not investigate the principal claimant's allegations and prosecute XXXX if they were all reported to them and the principal claimant agreed to follow through with them. I find that the claimants have not provided clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in Mexico is inadequate.

I would be remiss if I did not acknowledge and consider that there is information in the documentation to indicate that inefficiency, bribery and corruption remain issues in Mexican security forces at all levels, as well as within the public service sector. However, weighed against this is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to rectify the corruption and impunity that exists.

The Board accepts that Mexico has had some difficulties in the past with addressing the criminality and corruption that exist within the security forces in Mexico. The Board recognizes that there are some inconsistencies among several sources within the documentary evidence; however, the preponderance of the objective evidence regarding current country conditions suggests that, although not perfect, there is adequate state protection in Mexico for victims of crime, that Mexico is making serious efforts to address the problems of criminality, and that the police are both willing and able to protect victims. Police corruption and deficiencies, although existing and noted by the Board, are not systemic. I am of the view in canvassing the documentary evidence, that, as a whole, the issues of corruption and deficiencies are being addressed by the state of Mexico. The law provides criminal penalties for official corruption; however, the World Bank's Worldwide Governance Indicators and other indices reflected that corruption remained a problem at all levels of government, as some public officials continued to perpetrate bureaucratic abuses and some criminal acts with impunity. Corruption at the most basic level involved paying bribes for routine services or in lieu of fines to administrative officials and security forces. More sophisticated and less apparent forms of corruption included overpaying for goods and services to provide payment to elected officials and political parties. By the end of the year, 16 SSP and PGR officials had been indicted for corruption since the government launched Operation Cleanup in July 2008; however, none had been convicted. During the year the Customs Agency relieved more than 700 employees and replaced them with vetted officials.30

Concerning the implementation of the government's legislative framework, there has been significant advancements, especially when reviewing the progress Mexico has made in the last decade. For instance, while he was president, President Fox made reducing public corruption a key goal of his administration, and he gained international recognition for his efforts.31 Since then, the Mexican government has introduced a number of significant reforms in its security forces to combat crime over the past number of years: First, the federal Office of the Attorney General (PGR) recently established a new police force, the Federal Investigative Police (AFI) which replaced the notoriously corrupt Federal Judicial Police (PJF)....Efforts to develop the AFI into a professional, corruption-free force for the investigation of federal crimes are ongoing. Second, the Federal Preventive Police (PFP) was created in 1999...to prevent and combat crime throughout the country. The PFP came under the direction of the federal Ministry of Public Security (SSP) and has been assuming greater authority in stages over time, as its budget has grown and as it has incorporated and reorganized police departments from other major agencies such as those for migration, treasury, and highways. Third, the Public Security Secretariat of the Federal District (SSP-DF) unlike the PFP and SSP, does not have national reach, but it does manage a combined force of over 90,000 officers in the Federal District (DF). The SSP-DF is charged with maintaining public order and safety in the centre of Mexico City, where public insecurity and crime rates are the highest in the nation. As a result, there have been concurrent efforts to increase accountability and improve police effectiveness....The most high-profile effort was Mexico City Mayor Andrés Obrador's decision in 2002 to contract former New York City Mayor Rudolph Giuliani as a consultant to the SSP-DF.32

Furthermore, starting in the previous decade, Mexico created a number of agencies to combat crime, the drug cartels and organized crime: First, the PGR's Special Anti-Organized Crime Unit (UEDO) appeared as a response to the phenomenon of organized crime. The Federal Law against Organized Crime (LFCDO) was passed in November 1996 to deal with the problem of drug trafficking, though other crimes (such as migrant smuggling, trafficking in arms or infants, and terrorism) were covered in the LFCDO as well. Second, another unit within the PGR that has been important in the effort to combat drug trafficking and organized crime is the Office of the Special Prosecutor for Crimes against Health (FEADS). A third special office of the PGR is the Office of the Deputy Attorney for Special Investigation of Organized Crime (SIEDO). As currently organized, SIEDO contains six special units for investigating specific types of crimes: crimes against public health; terrorism and arms trafficking; money laundering and counterfeiting; human trafficking in minors, organs, and undocumented people; kidnappings; and robbery and other theft. The special offices of the PGR demonstrate the general rule that Mexican policing institutions try to reorganize themselves in a rational way to respond effectively to specific crime problems.33 A law approved on May 29 created a new federal investigative police force, the Federal Ministerial Police (PFM), which falls under the command of the Attorney General's Office. The PFM replaces the Attorney General's Federal Investigative Agency. Additionally, on April 30, Congress passed a new Federal Police Law that strengthens the Federal Police, which falls under SSP authority, and gives it limited investigative and intelligence-gathering abilities.34
The examples I have previously mentioned indicate that on the whole, in the past decade, Mexico has undertaken significant efforts to provide better protection for its citizens.

Further documentary evidence indicates that the security forces have instituted new recruiting procedures, drug testing, economic incentives, education and certification of officers, with sanctions levied against ineffective or corrupt officers, including arrests, prosecutions and convictions of Members of the security forces.35 The new government laws attacking corruption and bribery have resulted in sentences of five to 10 years' imprisonment for convicted officials, which have reportedly had a marked effect.36

Admittedly, corruption continued to be a problem, as many police, particularly at the state and local level, were involved in kidnapping, extortion, or providing protection for, or acting directly on behalf of, organized crime and drug traffickers. Impunity was pervasive and contributed to the continued reluctance of many victims to file complaints. Relating to this, documentary evidence indicates that: President Calderon remarked in speeches in March [2009] and October [2009] that corruption was a serious problem in the police forces and a primary reason for the use of the military in the domestic counternarcotics fight. The CNDH reported that police, especially at the state and local level, were involved in kidnapping, extortion, and in providing protection for, or acting directly on behalf of, organized crime and drug traffickers. Local forces in particular tended to be poorly compensated and directly pressured by criminal groups, leaving them most vulnerable to infiltration. According to a 2009 HRW report in impunity in the country, impunity was pervasive; this lack of accountability contributed to the continued reluctance of many victims to file complaints. Responsibility for investigating federal police abuse falls under the purview of the PGR or the Secretariat of Public Administration, depending on the type of offense. To better manage the corruption problem, in January the government enacted legislation establishing a four-year deadline to vet personnel in all of the country's 2,600 police forces using a series of testing mechanisms. The legislation requires all police forces to meet certain compensation and training standards, and it also makes it easier for authorities to fire corrupt or unfit officers. In addition to rooting out corruption at the federal level through "Operation Cleanup," the government led anticorruption operations in several states. On May 26, federal authorities arrested 10 mayors, a judge, and 16 law enforcement officers in the state of Michoacan for ties to drug trafficking. At least 12 of these officials were later released for lack of evidence against them. SSP officers arrested 92 police officers in the state of Hidalgo on June 26 for protecting a DTO. Also in June the military arrested more than 70 local and state law enforcement officers with presumed ties to organized crime. The CNDH received 14,633 complaints during the year, including 2,178 complaints against the SSP, which upon investigation produced a finding of 667 violations in categories that included arbitrary detention (244), noncompliance with arrest warrant procedures (177), and cruel and inhuman treatment (245). Significantly more than half the complaints received were resolved by inter alia reorienting the complainant to the proper authority (1,722), suspending an investigation for lack of evidence (222), and reaching an amicable agreement (49). Three complaints involving violations pertaining to treatment in prison and arbitrary detention resulted in recommendations calling on the SSP to make amends with victims and adopt procedural measures to comply with its obligations. In seeking to improve human rights practices, the SSP during the year conducted 131 courses specifically on human rights or with modules pertaining to the topic, training a total of 19,048 personnel. In the SSP training academy in San Luis Potosi, human rights were institutionalized as a standard part of the curriculum. The SSP also worked with the International Organization for Migration to hold three courses training 112 federal police officers. With experts from the ICRC, the SSP held two courses to train 24 personnel. Additionally, the CNDH trained 4,344 SSP officials. The SSP in collaboration with the National Autonomous University of Mexico also continued to provide human rights training to federal police officers throughout the country. Separately, the CNDH 2009 provided training to approximately 3,600 PGR personnel.37

Additional documentary evidence indicates that on October 27, 2008, Attorney General Medina Mora announced that five senior officials from the PGR's anti-organized crime unit (SIEDO) had been arrested for passing information to a major drug cartel. On October 31, 2008, Acting Federal Police (PFP) Commissioner Gerardo Garay Cardena resigned over allegations of his connections to the Sinaloa drug cartel; subsequently, he was arrested on corruption charges. Dozens more junior federal security officials have also been suspended or fired over corruption charges.38 In June 2007, the government of Mexico suspended 284 police officers from the PFP and AFI, including 34 state and Federal District police chiefs pending probes into their possible links to organized crime or drug trafficking.39 In July 2006, local police in the southern state of Tabasco unknowingly arrested Mateo Diaz Lopez, believed to be a leader of the Zetas.40 Further documentary evidence41 indicates that concerned that violent drug traffickers had infiltrated the police force, Mexican soldiers disarmed 149 local policemen assigned to the municipality of Rosario, Baja California, on December 28, 2007. Besides stripping local policemen of their weapons, the Baja California State Office of the Attorney General ordered all its Rosario personnel reassigned to other posts including Tijuana and Ensenada. In April 2007 over 100 state police officers in the northern state of Nuevo Leon were suspended due to corruption concerns. In June 2007, President Calderon purged 284 federal police commanders, including federal commanders of all 31 states and the federal district.42 These commanders were suspended and subjected to drug and polygraph tests. The Mexican government immediately named replacements for the 284 dismissed commanders. All of these actions indicate that Mexico is making serious effort to combat corruption.

Mexico has had problems in the past in dealing with domestic violence and violence against women. However, there is persuasive evidence that indicates that Mexico candidly acknowledges its past problems and is making serious efforts to deal with these issues.

With respect to domestic violence and violence against women, Mexico has enacted civil, administrative and criminal legislation which prohibits domestic violence and there are sanctions for transgressions which include detention or fines.43 In December 2006, in response to the recommendations on domestic abuse of many human rights organizations, Mexico enacted federal legislation which specifically addressed violence against women. The General Law on Women's Access to a Life Free of Violence requires federal and local authorities to prevent, punish and eradicate violence against women.44 In addition, many states have laws of their own prohibiting domestic violence such as the Federal District and Guadalajara. There is a special federal prosecutor for crimes against women and a cabinet-level National Institute of Women, which initiated a hotline for female victims of domestic abuse. Mexico has government-supported shelters, which offer psychological, legal and medical assistance. More than one source suggests that domestic violence is widespread, but that victims fail to report abuse for a number of reasons, including fear of becoming economically destitute if the perpetrator is convicted and fear of reprisal by the perpetrator.45 The Mexican Association for Violence Against Women reports that, to date, women have had little information about the remedies that are available to them. The recently enacted legislation makes victim awareness and general education of the public an entrenched part of the efforts to reverse previous domestic abuse trends. Due to the lack of awareness and insufficient legislation and enforcement, many women would opt for civil or administrative resolutions to address the violence they experienced and judges and prosecutors would direct attempts at conciliation and arbitration, rather than proceeding and sanctioning criminally.46

Importantly, the new legislation allows victims to seek protective or restraining orders, and gives police the authority to remove the aggressor from the home, gives exclusive possession of the residence to the victim, can require immediate child support provisions, allows police to seize firearms and provides the victim with immediate assistance.47 National health centres are required to report cases of domestic abuse to competent authorities and to provide rehabilitation of abusers. Physicians must report suspected cases to the public prosecutor. 48

The measures that have been taken, as mentioned above, indicate that Mexico is serious about combating domestic violence and violence against women. Some of the measures, such as the legislation that gives police the authority to remove the aggressor from the home, are reflected in the principal claimant's evidence.
I have considered the documentary evidence49 submitted by counsel with respect to state protection in Mexico.

The amnestyusa.org article Protection law fails Mexican women reports that a law to protect women in Mexico has had no impact in the two years since its inception. Also reported is that of the 30 states that have passed the law, only five have complied with the obligation to establish implementation mechanisms, only 20 have an agency coordination mechanism for preventing violence against women and only two new shelters for domestic violence victims are being built by state authorities. It is also indicated in the article that the federal government has, through INMUJERES, prioritized a harmonization of state legislation with national and international regulations.

In Judith Adler Hellman's Report on Human Rights in Mexico, the author describes the corruption that exists in Mexico, as well as public attitudes and perceptions relating to the effectiveness of state protection in Mexico, which confirms the professor's personal experience over the years. Professor Hellman states that no well-informed person would approach police for assistance in Mexico pointing to the years of impunity, abuse and corruption. She states that because of the deep seated problems, crimes, particularly those related to the narco traffickers are unlikely to be investigated. Professor Hellman acknowledges that Mexico has made a major shift towards a more open, transparent and democratic society although she does question the extent to how much it has actually done so.

However, despite Professor Hellman's report, the documentary evidence indicates the numerous, repeated and successful identification, investigations, arrests and prosecutions of even highly ranked government officials. Ultimately, the question is whether the protection offered in Mexico is adequate, and Professor Hellman's report does not define or address what adequacy of protection exists in Mexico. In Professor Hellman's report, the author makes statements such as "Mexicans have no recourse to the police for protection from wrongdoers as we do in Canada" and "It basically makes no sense to call on the police to rescue oneself from harm." I give little weight to this evidence as I find that the author makes general, sweeping statements regarding state protection in Mexico with little empirical data to back up her findings. For example, the author does not address facts such as the 224,749 prisoners in 440 facilities in Mexico.50 Furthermore, the author's personal experiences are contradicted by other documentary evidence and the principal claimant's own experiences.

In Alicia Elena Perez Duarte Y Norona's declaration, she concludes the following: Gender-based violence in Mexico occurs on a variety of levels: in the home at the hands of an abuser, tolerated and perpetuated by traditional social attitudes, and by a judicial system that is ineffective, which neither responds to nor has the political will to protect abused women and children. Each one of these spheres reinforces the idea that violence by a man against a woman is normal and expected. From my perspective, which is based upon more than thirty years of working on these issues, Mexico continues to be a patriarchal and misogynistic society with tiny changes of consciousness which are nearly invisible compared to the tolerance and the negligence of officials responsible for enforcing the laws.

I give little weight to this evidence. The author makes general sweeping statements about domestic violence and violence against women and children in Mexico with little empirical data to support her views. Furthermore, her views are contradicted by the principal claimant's experience with the authorities in Mexico where she received quite meticulous attention when it was requested, which I find amounts to adequate protection.

Having considered the reports of Professor Hellman and Alicia Elena Perez Duarte Y Norona as well as other equally or even more persuasive and current reports, which include information and references, I have assigned lesser weight to the Hellman and Norona reports for these deficiencies. Counsel has also included many articles about domestic abuse and gender violence issues and cases from Mexico and around the world. I accept that many countries around the world struggle to deal effectively with these issues, however, many countries, such as Mexico, have enacted laws to combat domestic violence and violence against women and have put in place measures to ensure that the laws are enforced.

Therefore, having considered the totality of the evidence, I find that the claimants, in the circumstances of this case, have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence and that the claimants did not take all reasonable steps in the circumstances to avail themselves of that protection before making claims for refugee protection. Therefore, I am not persuaded that the state of Mexico would not be reasonably forthcoming with state protection, should the claimants seek it.

There is no persuasive evidence before me that the claimants would face a serious possibility of persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to their life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or a risk of torture, if they returned to Mexico. For all these reasons, I find that that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the Act, as state protection is available to them.

As the minor claimant bases her claim on that of the principal claimant, her mother, and membership in a particular social group, namely, the family, and no persuasive evidence was adduced to differentiate her claim from that of her mother's, her claim must also fail.

I determine that the claimants are neither Convention refugees nor persons in need of protection. The Refugee Protection Division therefore rejects their claims. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
